hero.name: Kunal
hero.who: a CA student in Indore who watches slower classmates overtake him

story.b: In school, Kunal was the boy who finished maths tests first. Teachers in Indore called him a natural with numbers. Now he is two years into CA, and the intermediate results are out. He has cleared one group and failed the other. His classmate Pooja, who used to borrow his notes in Class 11, has cleared both. Kunal sits at the poha stall near Rajwada and scrolls through the congratulations in the class group. He knows exactly what happened. Whenever a chapter got boring, he switched to another. Whenever a mock test went badly, he took a week off. Pooja just kept showing up at the library at eight every morning. Kunal starts searching for MBA courses on his phone.

ask.q: Kunal is thinking of quitting CA after failing one group. What is the most useful thing to look at first?
o: Whether he has the natural talent CA really needs
How steadily he has worked, compared with how talented he is
Which new course looks easier and more exciting
ask.why: Kunal clearly has the talent. His problem was stopping whenever the work got dull or hard. Questioning his talent misses that, and jumping to a shiny new course repeats the same pattern. Looking honestly at his steadiness shows him what to fix.

chapters.take: Talent gets you started. Steady effort decides who finishes.

story.b: Kunal decides to give CA one honest year before thinking about anything else. He writes the goal on an index card and tapes it inside his cupboard: become a chartered accountant, however long it takes. Then comes costing, the subject he finds dullest. For the first week he goes to the library at eight, like Pooja, and feels nothing but boredom. In the second week his college friends plan a four-day trip to Mandu and ask him to come. Kunal is tempted. Instead he joins them for one evening of dal bafla and heads back to his books. By the end of the month, costing is still not exciting, but he has finished it properly for the first time in two years.

ask.q: Kunal feels nothing but boredom in week two. What should he do?
o: Keep turning up daily, since steady effort through dull weeks is what counts
Wait until he feels motivated again, then study twice as hard
Switch to a subject he enjoys more and come back later
ask.why: Boring weeks are part of any long goal, and waiting for motivation lets them win. Switching subjects is the exact habit that stalled him before. Showing up anyway turns his talent into real skill, one dull day at a time.

chapters.take: Long goals are won on the boring days, not the exciting ones.

story.b: In his next mock test, Kunal loses most of his marks on one type of question: GST calculations with tricky exemptions. His old habit would be to re-read the whole tax book from page one, which feels productive and changes little. This time he picks only those questions. He solves five a day under a timer at the library. Every Saturday he shows his answers to Mehta sir, a retired CA who helps students for free at the community hall. Mehta sir circles the same mistake three weeks running, a wrong rate in one step. It is embarrassing. Kunal writes the rule on a sticky note and solves twenty more until he stops making it. In the next mock test, that section is his strongest.

ask.q: Kunal's friend Rohan has also failed tax. Which plan would help him improve fastest?
o: Read the full tax book again from the start
Study longer hours every day across all chapters
Find his weakest question type, practise it with feedback, and repeat
ask.why: Re-reading feels busy but rarely fixes a specific mistake, and simply adding hours spreads effort thin. Picking one weak spot, practising it with full focus and getting someone to point out errors is uncomfortable, and that discomfort is where skill grows.

chapters.take: Practise your weakest spot on purpose, with feedback, until it stops being weak.

story.b: One mock test goes badly, and Kunal comes home convinced he is stupid. His father is at the counter of their small hardware shop, frowning at a notice about a late tax filing. The accountant they pay has stopped answering calls. Kunal sits down, reads the notice and sorts it out in an hour. His father pats his shoulder and says the whole lane needs someone like him. That night Kunal thinks about the tea stall owner, the tailor and the kirana uncle next door, all confused by the same forms. He opens the mock paper again. Instead of deciding he is stupid, he writes down what went wrong: he rushed the long questions. Tomorrow he will try a new method.

ask.q: After a bad mock test, which thought will help Kunal keep going?
o: I am just not smart enough for this exam
I need a better method, and this work will help people like Papa
I should stop taking mock tests so they cannot upset me
ask.why: Calling himself stupid turns one result into a fixed verdict, and avoiding mocks hides the information he needs. Believing a better method will help gives him hope, and remembering the traders who need him gives him a reason to keep trying.

chapters.take: Purpose gives you a reason to go on. Hope tells you it can work.

story.b: Kunal never imagined he would enjoy audit. It sounded like ticking boxes. But at his articleship firm, his senior, Fatima didi, hands him the stock records of a local sweets distributor and asks him to find out why the numbers do not match. For two days it is tedious. On the third day he spots a pattern: returns entered twice during festival weeks. He feels a small thrill, like solving a puzzle. Fatima didi gives him a harder file. Then another. Slowly, without deciding to, he starts reading audit cases on the bus home. His younger sister Neha, in Class 11, complains that she has no passion and everyone else has found theirs. Kunal laughs. He is still finding his.

ask.q: Neha says she has no passion and is scared she never will. What should Kunal tell her?
o: Try a few things she is mildly curious about, then stay with one and let interest grow
Wait patiently until the right passion appears one day
Pick whatever career pays the most and forget about passion
ask.why: Passion rarely arrives fully formed, so waiting for it can last forever. Ignoring interest altogether makes the long years harder. Exploring a little, then committing and building small wins, is how mild curiosity usually deepens into real passion, just as audit did for Kunal.

chapters.take: Interest grows from small wins and time. Explore first, then commit.

story.b: Four months before the next attempt, Kunal notices that his worst days are the ones he spends with the gang from the chai tapri near his house. They are fun, but they joke about anyone who studies on a Saturday. So he asks Pooja if he can join her group at the library. There are five of them. They start at eight, test each other at noon over poha and share the hardest questions in a single chat group with no memes allowed. Mehta sir drops by on Saturdays, warm but strict, and never lets anyone off easy. On days Kunal feels lazy, he goes anyway, because the others are already there. Effort feels normal in that room, and that makes everything easier.

ask.q: Kunal's cousin wants to start running but keeps stopping after a week. What would help most?
o: Rely on willpower alone, because grit should come from inside
Run with friends who joke that exercise is a waste of time
Join a regular running group where showing up is normal
ask.why: Willpower alone is easy to lose on a tired morning, and friends who mock effort quietly pull you back. A group where everyone shows up makes effort feel normal, and warm but demanding people help you stretch without giving up.

chapters.take: Stand near people who work hard. Their effort becomes your normal.

story.b: Kunal sits the exam again in May with a calm he has never felt before. He does not know if he will pass, and for once that is not the main thing. He has studied every subject fully, including the dull ones. He still solves five weak questions every morning, still meets the eight o'clock group and still helps the traders on his father's lane with their forms on Sundays. When the results come, he has cleared it. Pooja sends a sticker of a dancing goat. Neha has joined a weekend coding class, unsure if she likes it yet, but going. The MBA tabs on Kunal's phone were closed long ago. The index card is still taped inside his cupboard.

chapters.take: Grit is not a gift. It is built one ordinary day at a time.
